newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate panel passes juvenile crime bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate panel passes juvenile crime bill.

text.p: The Senate Judiciary Committee Thursday passed a tough new juvenile crime bill, which includes provisions that would treat and punish young violent criminals like adults.

The bill passed 12-6 but several of the leading Democrats on the panel, including Joseph Biden of Delaware and Herbert Kohl of Wisconsin, vowed to fight on the Senate floor for several key provisions including requiring guns to be equipped with child safety locks, and gun control aimed at juvenile offenders.

Attorney General Janet Reno said the legislation was a step in the right direction but failed to include many important provisions needed to ensure a balanced approach. She said she hoped to work with Congress to improve the bill.
Committee chairman Orrin Hatch said the bill "is about accountability" and aims to crack down fast and hard on violent offenders even when they are young.

"No one wants to have to sentence a juvenile to a lengthy prison term," Hatch said. "But if a juvenile has committed a crime as heinous as that committed by the worst adult criminal, we must do this to protect society."
The bill gives federal prosecutors the option of trying juveniles as adults. A juvenile could not be housed in the same cell as an adult offender in federal cases.
Most criminal cases, however, are local not federal, but the bill has a variety of grants for states to fight juvenile crime. It also has stronger anti-gang provisions.

Democratic critics, however, said the state programmes do not place enough emphasis on prevention. Biden said he supports locking up the truly violent youth, who may number 100,000, but wants to ensure there are adequate prevention programmes for youths who are "not lost to us yet but clearly are falling deeper into the crime stream."

Gun control activist Sarah Brady has also criticised the Senate Judiciary Committee's decision to drop a child safety lock provision from the legislation, citing recent Justice Department studies that 55 percent of all handguns in the United States were kept unloaded and unlocked.

A recent study by the General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, found that all unintentional firearm deaths of children 6 and under could be prevented with properly installed child locks.
Children unintentionally fire guns 10,000 times each year, resulting in at least 800 deaths, Brady said.

Reno said the legislation needed to ensure that juveniles were housed separately from adults in the the state juvenile systems so that "those who come in as delinquents will not leave as hardened criminals."
